Application Areas: Conservation of aerial insectivores and swallows
Delineation of ecologically distinct management groups
Annual cycle management of migratory species
Key Research Thinking Patterns: AI-Driven Radar Phenotyping: Leveraging spatiotemporal convolutional neural networks (e.g., Faster R-CNN with Kalman Filtering) to automatically detect and track communal bird roosts in NEXRAD weather radar data, enabling the extraction of thousands of roost signatures for large-scale ecological analysis.

Multi-Scale Environmental Coupling: Integrating high-resolution gridded weather variables with long-term radar observations to identify how local proximate drivers (e.g., headwinds) and distant distal factors (e.g., breeding site temperature) jointly influence avian migration timing and roosting phenology.

Connectivity-Based Management Delineation: Combining satellite tracking data (Argos/GPS) with unsupervised clustering and migratory connectivity metrics to define ecologically distinct management units, moving beyond traditional flyway boundaries to address population declines in species like the long-billed curlew.

Hybrid Data Validation Frameworks: Pairing automated weather radar detection pipelines with community-science observations (eBird) to validate species-specific contributions to radar echoes, distinguishing between primary targets (swallows/martins) and secondary contributors (grackles/starlings) in nocturnal migration monitoring.
Summary Description: Jeffrey Kelley is an aeroecologist specializing in the large-scale monitoring of avian migration and communal roosting using weather radar and machine learning. His research integrates computer vision (CNNs) with spatiotemporal analysis of NEXRAD data to automate the detection of bird movements, significantly advancing the study of declining aerial insectivores. He employs multi-scale environmental modeling to link local weather conditions with distant climatic drivers affecting phenology. Additionally, Kelley utilizes satellite tracking and connectivity metrics to delineate effective management units for conservation. His work bridges computational science and ornithology, providing robust tools for monitoring migratory connectivity and informing conservation strategies for swallows, martins, and curlews.
